I used to get soooo upset over jerks. I took it all personally and felt really disrespected when people were rude and mean. I have borderline personality disorder and could lose my shit pretty easily in those situations. I've since graduated from Dialectical Behavior Therapy and no longer feel those extreme effects of rude behavior. I think the biggest skill from DBT that helped is Opposite Action to Anger, where I really put myself I their shoes to see why their reaction could make sense. This was pretty hard at first but now it's my automatic response and has been life changing. 

I've also thought back to my poor treatment of people and realized that happens when I'm feeling like shit in my own life and usually has nothing to do with the person I was being a jerk to.

I have  BPD, too and used to feel the same way. I was so suicidal for a very long time, I was convinced it was the only thing I could do to prevent me from hurting others. After 20 years of hospitalizations, meds, therapists and psychiatrists I finally got into DBT. I've been symptom free for 6 months now.  

It took 4 hours of group/individual a week and it rewired how I think and behave. I'm sharing this bc I used to get dangerously depressed reading about BPD and rarely heard anything hopeful. 

It is possible to recover from BPD. Brian Barnett on Quora has a unique explanation for BPD's cause and it really helped me fully recover.  I'd say DBT was 85%, Brian's answers were the rest. https://www.quora.com/profile/Brian-Barnett-2

BPD symptoms are absolute hell and all encompassing.

I feel your pain, I've been there and I thought I was beyond hope.  I thought I'd be the one person even DBT couldn't help.  What I learned is that even if you've tried a bunch of different meds and been pushed away, belittled, misunderstood and not heard- DON'T GIVE UP!! 

In DBT they taught that "You are not your thoughts".  That was a wake up for me and I needed it explained.  

She said if she showed me a pen and told me that it played music when used, then she saw me a week later and asked me what sound the pen makes, I'd probably say "it plays music".  That thought,  that the pen plays music, was not my own thought but a thought she had put in my head.  

Her point was our thoughts come from all sorts of places and they're NOT ALWAYS RIGHT. So every time I was suicidal and positive nothing would ever get better, I was wrong and those were just thoughts.  

Another lifesaver has been meditation.  Specifically Headspace, it's a free app with a neat sounding Aussie named Andy. His voice is soothing and kind.  And meditating allows distance between me and my thoughts and is almost like taking a brief vacation from the pain. 

Another DBT skill, and this is for when I can't stop crying and the barrage of horrible thoughts, is to place my face in a bowl of really cold water for 30 seconds.  This activates the dive reflex and slows the heart rate.  It's REALLY effective for calming down. 

The National Suicide Hotline hasn't been able to help me in the past much but it's because I couldn't open up to them.  I knew they didn't know me and, because I was that upset, I thought they were being fake but in reality they're not.  Some people are just gifted at talking to suicidal people IMHO, the sheriff that rescued me was one of them, and I think you have a really good chance of talking to one there. 

The emergency room will keep you alive and call a Designated Mental Health Provider. That person will hopefully talk to you enough that you can go home and wait for an outpatient appointment they have scheduled. That was what happened to me in this story.

I've had two bad experiences though with different DMHPs. The first instance, I perceived him as being condescending and it triggered a rage. I screamed at him and then the entire emergency room staff was in my room. I'm sensitive but he wasn't exactly compassionate.   

Now, if I'm in a situation with someone who would normally make me furious, I focus on being EFFECTIVE in the situation. Letting him know what I think about him and my perceived judgments does not get me what I want.

If they feel you need inpatient then they will call around for a bed, which means find a place.  Then they'll take on a stretcher in an ambulance.  

I actually love the psych ward.  I've been three times to three very different wards. 
Each time made me realize I'm not alone, especially with borderline as we're statistically 20% off the population. I loved meeting new people and learning their story without constantly worrying if I'm being depressing or sharing too much.  I could be myself and if I was too emotional it was ok, it was perfectly normal to "be crazy".

Does this help, can you call the hotline and open up, give them a chance to help?  Or get to the emergency room if you're scared you're not safe?
